claim_grade: B-claim (empirical reduced-form evidence + calibrated model simulation; the model results are conditional on structural assumptions, not observed policy). Tier 1: peer-reviewed in Real Estate Economics. Author standing judged by the rubric, none of the names is in sources/audit/people-tiers.json: Cho has peer-reviewed housing-tax OLG work (Cho, Li & Uren, Quantitative Economics 2024 and International Economic Review 2024, both cited in the paper's own references); Park is at KDI School; Zhang is at Jinan University (Unpaywall/Crossref affiliation for the published paper; the 2025 WP lists Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia). Unpaywall lists Cho at Sogang University for the published version while WPs list Jinan University -- T1 should confirm affiliations before writing them.
content_summary: PUBLISHED ABSTRACT (Crossref, verified verbatim source): reduced-form evidence that Shanghai's pilot 'had little impact on the overall housing market, with suggestive evidence of a reduction in the unit prices of larger homes'; a general-equilibrium overlapping-generations model of housing and rental markets with heterogeneous agents, calibrated to China, compares universal and targeted property taxes. Three results: (1) the universal tax reduces house prices and raises rents; (2) higher rents and ongoing tax burden make housing services less affordable, though low-income households benefit more from redistribution of the extra revenue; (3) universal taxes give a long-run welfare gain (driven by redistribution and lower prices), but 'along the transition, 55% of existing households experience a welfare loss'; 'poorer households gain and richer households lose'. PILOT DESIGN (Lincoln Institute article, Tier 1 body): from 28 Jan 2011 Shanghai taxed newly purchased second homes of residents and first (new) homes of non-residents on transaction value after excluding 60 m2 per person; Chongqing taxed existing single-family homes and new luxury apartments (exclusions of 180 m2 / 100 m2). The paper's own description is looser: Shanghai 'second homes at 0.6%'; Chongqing 0.5% (1% above RMB 15,000/m2) on investment and high-end (>140 m2) homes. My recollection (NOT verified here) is that the official Shanghai rate was 0.4% or 0.6% applied to 70% of transaction value -- T1 should check against an official/Tier 1 source before stating rates beyond 'up to 0.6%'. REDUCED FORM (July 2025 WP, not the published version): synthetic difference-in-differences, city-quarter panel, Shanghai vs Beijing, Tianjin, Ningbo, Guangzhou, Hangzhou, Wuhan, CREIS new-home transaction data; ATT on log price -0.003 to -0.021 and on area per transaction +0.002 to +0.010, all statistically insignificant (Table 2). Price effects modestly negative for ~18 months then rising, none significant. It cites Du & Zhang (2015: no effect) and Zheng & Zhang (2013: -RMB 2,127/m2, -13.4%, synthetic control) and says the difference may reflect design and period. The published 'larger homes' suggestive result and its size are not in the WP and could not be retrieved. MODEL (July 2025 WP numbers; may have changed in the published version, which reports 55% vs the WP's 58%): universal 0.5% tax -- house price -3.7%, rent +2.8%, price-to-rent -6.3%; targeted (investment housing only) -- price +0.3%, rent +5.5%, housing investment about -30%. Steady-state newborn welfare (consumption-equivalent variation): +0.69% universal, -0.42% targeted; redistribution of the extra revenue is the key mechanism (without redistribution the universal tax lowers welfare). Transition (unexpected permanent reform): average welfare -0.13% in both; about 42% (universal) and 23% (targeted) of surviving households gain; under universal tax welfare falls monotonically in wealth, renters and younger/poorer households gain, older/richer owners and landlords lose. Policy conclusion (WP): a targeted (investment-property) tax fails to curb prices and lowers welfare; a universal tax lowers prices but worsens affordability unless revenue is rebated; 'redistributing the additional tax revenue' is decisive; the authors note a national tax remains under discussion after the 2023 slump. GEORGIST RELEVANCE: this is a recurrent tax on housing value (land + structures), and the lump-sum rebate result parallels the citizen's-dividend logic, but the paper says nothing about land value specifically.
existing_wiki_coverage: Not in the wiki (grep of the repo for 'Cho, Park', 'Taxing Homeowners', 'Zheng and Zhang', 'Du and Zhang' finds only LOOPLOG hits unrelated). Neighbours (read): research/liu-shanghai-chongqing-property-tax-pilots.md (Liu 2026, synthetic control, finds lower price-to-income ratios in both cities, abstract-level, Journal of Applied Economics and Social Dynamics -- a direct tension with Cho et al.'s null price result that the wiki should surface), research/hou-kumhof-shao-china-lvt-simulation.md (DSGE LVT simulation, land-lease context), research/xu-china-land-finance-active-mode.md (land finance / lease-sale system, distinct from recurrent property tax; the Liu page already draws that distinction). No places/china.md exists; no China property-tax concept page.
uncertainties: 1) Published-version numbers unverified: only the abstract is confirmed; the WP magnitudes (3.7%, 2.8%, 0.69%, 58%) may differ from the published version (abstract already shows 55%). 2) The 'larger homes' finding and its magnitude are unknown. 3) Shanghai rate/base details: two sources give different levels of detail; check an official source. 4) Tension with Liu (2026) is real (Liu: improved affordability; Cho et al.: little price effect) and the two use different outcome variables (price-to-income vs price/area) and controls; do not present either as settled. 5) Authors' affiliations differ across versions. 6) Queue context says SSRN 4995324; a second SSRN id 5350298 also appears in search results for the same title.

It is a quasi-experimental difference-in-differences estimate; the 'full capitalization eventually' reading rests on an assumed range of discount rates (the authors say capitalization and discount rate cannot be separately identified).
content_summary: SETTING: City-owned land in Helsinki leased for ~60-year terms in the 1950s-60s with rents indexed to the cost-of-living index, so rents became 'negligible' relative to market rents. In the condominium system the housing company is the lessee and land rent is bundled into monthly maintenance fees, so the cost is 'nontransparent' to buyers. Finnish law gives lessees a right to renew but sets no maximum rent or increase. From 2010 large-scale renewals began. In January 2008 Helsinki announced that renewal rent would be about 4% of the land value appraised by independent experts (the ERES 2023 abstract says 'over 15-fold rent increases'; the published paper says 'multifold' and 'over a 40% rise in operating costs'). After political pressure the increase was phased in: 50% at renewal, then +5% of the total each year to the full level after 10 years; renewed term 50 years, still CPI-indexed. INFORMATION SHOCK: the paper's Figure A1 shows essentially no media coverage before the Jan 2008 announcement; later announcements (first estimate Feb 2017, precise unit-level estimate Dec 2017, information events Jan 2018, City Council confirmation spring 2018) refined it. Study batch: the 2021 renewals (>700 lots). DATA/DESIGN: 10,984 condominium sales in Helsinki 2003-2021 (4,545 leasehold, 6,439 freehold; buildings built 1957-63, same neighbourhoods; agent-brokered sales covering ~70% of transactions); average expected rise in unit maintenance cost EUR 1,130/yr (range 375-3,693). Difference-in-differences of leasehold vs near-identical freehold units; rents of the two groups show no differential (no unobserved-quality gap). RESULTS: no leasehold discount before 2008 (2007 baseline -0.009, s.e. 0.018; pre-trend tests insignificant): buyers ignored the future rent rise. No immediate reaction to the 2008 announcement. Pooled estimates (log price): 2008-2016 -0.052 (dummy) / -0.053 (per EUR 1,000 of rent increase), 2017-2021 -0.111 / -0.095, i.e. about -10.5% (EUR 28,331) and -9.1% (EUR 24,422) at the mean freehold price of EUR 269,565. Year-by-year, discounts stay small into the early 2010s, become large and significant from 2015, converge near 10%, and show no significant change between 2020 and 2021 when the new rents took effect, i.e. the rise was priced in before payment began. Present-value benchmarks (their Fig. 2): with perfect foresight the 2003 discount would have been 8.6/13.9/24.8% at 4/3/2% real discount rates; assuming no knowledge before 2008 and a 3% rate, an immediate -14.5% in 2008; in 2021 expected discounts 11.2/15.1/22.7%. Implied real discount rates from the final-period estimate: 2.45-2.48% (50-year horizon; 95% CI about 0.7-5.5%) and 3.68-3.70% (perpetuity; CI 2.7-6.0%), in line with Giglio et al. 2015 (2.6%), Bracke et al. 2018 (2-3%), Gautier & van Vuuren 2019 (4%, Amsterdam). MECHANISM: price dispersion of leasehold sales rose after 2008 and fell in 2021; the share of 'noncapitalized' transactions fell from 67-72% (2003-06) to about 30% (2018-21) while 'capitalized' rose; about 13% 'in-between'. Authors read this as a segmented market with heterogeneous attention, not a uniform slow adjustment; seller reservation-price stickiness is considered and judged unlikely to last so long. Robustness: alternative neighbourhood definitions; controls for the differential land-tax and mortgage-interest-deduction phase-out; a fully interacted specification attenuates the post-2017 discount to about -0.077/-0.079 but stays significant. IMPLICATION FOR LAND-RENT CAPITALIZATION: (1) an announced, credible, legally certain increase in a land-rent obligation is capitalized into prices, roughly fully at a 2.5-3.7% discount rate (in line with UK/Singapore/Amsterdam lease studies), supporting the standard present-value picture; (2) but the timing is slow -- about a decade from announcement to a stable discount -- when the charge is bundled and nontransparent, which qualifies the wiki's shorthand that unanticipated changes capitalize 'at announcement' and bears on transition design and on how visible a land-rent charge should be. Authors note the setting is a lease, 'similar to property or other taxes', not a tax, and Finnish effective property tax is low, so differential tax is small. Quotable (<=50 words; abstract): 'The leasehold discount increase is substantially slower than predicted by the present value model, implying only partial adjustment over the short run, but is in line with full capitalization eventually.'
existing_wiki_coverage: Not in the wiki. concepts/tax-capitalization.md (read in full) has Oates, Palmon & Smith, Danish land-tax study (full capitalization), Borge & Rattso, Hilber, Buettner, Tubio-Sanchez, and an 'Anticipation matters' caveat that 'Only unanticipated tax changes are cleanly capitalized at announcement' -- the Helsinki paper is a direct empirical complication of that line and adds the first slow-capitalization / information-diffusion case. concepts/public-land-leasing.md covers Hong Kong, Singapore, Canberra, Ethiopia; Finland appears only inside a sentence citing Bourassa & Hong (2003). concepts/ground-rent.md has the economic vs contract ground-rent distinction (UK Leasehold Reform (Ground Rent) Act 2022) but no municipal-lessor example. research/lyytikainen-finland-three-rate.md (read in full) is the only Finnish page; its See Also lists split-rate and Pennsylvania pages only. No places/finland.md exists.
uncertainties: 1) Appendix figures/tables not viewed as images. 2) 'Over 15-fold' (ERES 2023 abstract) versus 'multifold'/'over 40% rise in operating costs' (published) -- use the published wording. 3) The 'full capitalization eventually' claim depends on assumed discount rates and an assumed rent path (phase-in, constant real land value growth 0.7% as in Giglio et al.); capitalization and discount rate are not separately identified (authors say so). 4) Single case: one city, one 2021 batch, older condominium stock, agent-brokered sales only. 5) Lease-contract rent is not a tax; transferring the timing result to LVT is an analogy the authors themselves only gesture at -- keep the wiki wording at 'bears on', not 'shows'. 6) Whether 'Falkenbach & Krigsholm (2026)' (cited for Finland's low effective property tax) is worth a separate look was not checked.

content_summary: Claims: replacing Council Tax and Stamp Duty with a Proportional Property Tax (PPT) 'would deliver a £10.1bn boost to high streets'; 'average council area could benefit by as much as £34.3m a year'; 279 of 295 English authorities net gains; average household saving £566; 'over three quarters of households' better off; County Durham top (average household saving £900/yr, £211m local spending), Leeds £170m, Sheffield £150m; 17 of the top 50 areas are places where Labour lost control in five years; category split (£2bn housing and fuel, £1.3bn transport, £1.2bn food, £1.2bn recreation, £680m restaurants/hotels, £601m household goods, £262m clothing); about £91m extra VAT from hotel and restaurant spending. Arithmetic check: £10.1bn / 295 = £34.2m, consistent with the £34.3m average. BASIS (release's own methodological note): uses 'Fairer Share's modelled average household gains from reform, based on 2020 data', recent ONS household counts and local income profiles; the spending uplift is allocated by national ONS Family Spending patterns; 'The model assumes full household gains are spent.' No author or independent reviewer is named; the release does not say what happens to prices, rents or the losers, and counts only gains to households. Polling: representative online poll of 2,048 UK adults, 1-4 Aug 2026, JL Partners (British Polling Council member): 63% regard Council Tax as unfair; 52% worry about affording next year's bills; 36% would spend savings on 'energy and other bills', 40% on 'food and other essentials'. NAMED PEOPLE: Andrew Dixon (Fairer Share founder; quoted: 'a Burnham boost'); Labour MPs Sam Rushworth (Bishop Auckland; Band D in County Durham vs Kensington & Chelsea), Paula Barker (Liverpool Wavertree), Chris Webb and Lorraine Beavers (Blackpool, joint statement 'punitive and unfair'), Jonathan Brash (Hartlepool; 'established the Fairer Council Tax Group' with a party-conference fringe event). The release says the Fairer Share petition for a review passed 100,000 signatures so MPs will 'likely' debate it, and that 'Andy Burnham became Prime Minister' after the government was 'already considering reform proposals'; it says Burnham 'has repeatedly endorsed property tax reform' but quotes no Burnham statement on this analysis -- 'Burnham boost' is the campaign's label. ADJACENT LEADS (from the same site, 28-29 Sept 2026): (a) the Resolution Foundation has proposed replacing Council Tax and Stamp Duty with a single revenue-neutral tax at 0.7% of current home value, paid by occupiers with rebates and deferral (Fairer Share's summary; the RF report itself was not fetched); figures quoted: UK property tax 3.7% of GDP in 2023 vs OECD average 2%, effective rate on a £100k home nearly 3x that on a £1m home by 2030-31, 61% of English households overpaying by £430 on average -- these should be taken from RF's own publication if queued; (b) 'Property Tax Lab' modelling (900,000+ valuations) said to find 83% of English dwellings pay less under a 0.48% PPT and Stamp Duty abolition would raise transactions about 8.8% (about 76,000 sales) and remove about £804m deadweight loss -- again second-hand via Fairer Share; primary not located.

Not on the InfoStride article alone: the article is thin (a single speaker, no figures on ground rent, generic housing-deficit and imported-materials numbers unsourced, and a stale event date). If T1 prefers not to open a country page for this, the fallback is a BACKLOG note: 'Nigeria: Land Use Act 1978 ground rent, Lagos Land Use Charge consolidation (Franzsen & McCluskey ch. 32; LUC Law 2018 primary text); NIESV advocacy'. My judgment is that the page is justified because the primary statute (A-claim) and a Tier 1 Lincoln Institute chapter are both in hand and Africa is thinly covered (places/ethiopia, south-africa, research on Kenya and the Franzsen book exist; Nigeria has only a rentier-state research page).
claim_grade: Land Use Act text: A-claim, Tier 1 (primary statute). Franzsen & McCluskey 2017 ch. 32: A/B-claim, Tier 1 (Lincoln Institute; that chapter's Nigeria section is itself based on Lincoln working papers by Jibao 2009). NIESV/InfoStride: C-claim (a professional body's advocacy reported by a Nigerian online outlet), Tier 2; usable for what NIESV said, never as evidence ground rent would work.
content_summary: WHAT NIESV SAID (per InfoStride): NIESV 'renewed its call' for ground rent as a revenue and housing-affordability strategy; speaker was Gbenga Ismail, chairman of the Lagos State chapter (other Nigerian outlets call him 'former chairman' of the Lagos branch, and his Estate Week remarks are reported for 2024/2025), speaking 'during the 2025 Estate Surveyors' Week held in Lagos' -- although the article is stamped 26 Sept 2026, so the event is about a year old. Proposal: government releases land 'at a marginal cost' and developers pay 'the bulk of their fees gradually through a structured ground rent system' (amortizing what would otherwise be an upfront land price); regular ground-rent payment, enforced with loss of land for non-compliance, would push owners to develop idle land. Direct quote: 'We cannot continue to price land in a way that shuts out the average Nigerian.' He also cited that over 70% of building materials are imported, backed Lagos State's proposed move from annual to monthly RENT payments (a private-tenancy matter unrelated to ground rent, needing a legal framework and a pilot in government estates), and suggested incentives for compliant landlords. The reporter adds a national housing deficit 'estimated at over 17 million units' (unsourced) and that 'experts believe' a transparent rent structure would reduce speculation. No revenue figures, rates, or Nigerian ground-rent collection data are given. LEGAL BASIS (Land Use Act 1978, FAOLEX text): s.1 -- 'all land comprised in the territory of each State in the Federation is hereby vested in the Governor of that State, and such land shall be held in trust and administered for the use and common benefit of all Nigerians'; s.2 -- urban land under the Governor's control, other land under local governments; s.5(1) -- the Governor may grant statutory rights of occupancy, 'demand rental for any such land', revise the rental at intervals in the certificate of occupancy or at any time if none are specified, and impose penal rent for breach of a covenant to develop; s.10 -- every certificate of occupancy is deemed to bind the holder to pay the rent fixed by the Governor and any revised rent; s.16 -- in fixing or revising rent the Governor must consider rents of neighbouring land and 'shall not take into consideration any value due to capital expended upon the land by the same or any previous occupier ... or any increase in the value of the land ... due to the employment of such capital' (an explicit land-not-improvements rent principle); s.17 -- rent-free or reduced-rent grants in the public interest, with a power to impose rent later; s.19 -- penal rent for failure to develop, capped at the rent reserved for the first year and at double the previous penal rent on revision, and revocation as an alternative; s.28 -- revocation for overriding public interest (with compensation provisions in Part V). TIER 1 CORROBORATION AND PRACTICE (Franzsen & McCluskey 2017, ch. 32): the Land Use Decree (1978) 'nationalized all land' and vested administration in state and local bodies, replacing prior titles with statutory (Governor-granted, mainly urban) and customary rights of occupancy; property tax (tenement rates) is a local-government tax on gross-rental-value-based ratable value and is 'generally overlooked' because councils rely on federation-account allocations; Lagos State in 2001 'rationalized several property taxes into a single property charge, the land use charge (LUC), ... to replace ... tenement rates, ground rents, and neighborhood improvement charges', assessed on capital value. (The 2018 Lagos LUC Law's contents, e.g. a bill payable by owner or short-lease occupier, are known to me only from law-firm summaries and a web search snippet, not the statute.) GEORGIST FIT: Nigeria's ground rent is statutory/contract rent under a state-held land regime, i.e. closer to public land leasing (see concepts/public-land-leasing.md and the ground-rent page's 'contract ground rent' sense) than to a land value tax; NIESV's proposal converts an upfront allocation price into a rent stream and makes non-payment a lever against idle land. Whether anything like s.16's land-only rent principle is applied in practice is not established by these sources.

Nigeria appears only in research/namo-nasarawa-solid-minerals-rentier-state.md (mineral governance, Nasarawa State) and, in passing, resource-rent pages. uncertainties: 1) Date: the InfoStride piece (26 Sept 2026) describes the 2025 Estate Week and other outlets place Ismail's remarks in 2024/2025; treat as an undated-to-2025 statement and do not present it as a current or new NIESV campaign. 2) The FAOLEX copy is the 1978 text; the current Act is Cap. L5 LFN 2004 and has been debated for amendment; section numbers quoted should be re-checked against the LFN 2004 text (placng.org and nigerianlawforum.com copies surfaced by search but were not read). 3) I recall the Act being entrenched in the 1999 Constitution (s.315(5)(d)) but did not verify it -- omit unless checked. 4) 'Ground rent' in the article is not defined by the speaker; the reporter's definition (periodic payment by leaseholders to government for the right to occupy and develop) is consistent with the Act's 'rental' but the article never cites the Act. 5) No evidence gathered on actual ground-rent collection or on the Lagos LUC's 2018 rates.
